correctness.rationale: The polar curvature numerator equals (1+eta cos 3theta)(1+10eta cos 3theta)+18eta^2 sin^2 3theta >0 for 0<=eta<1/10. The maximal-area triangle in the containing radius-(1+eta) disk is equilateral, and for eta>0 exactly the three radial bulges lie on its boundary, yielding six labeled maxima. Direct signed-area expansion has eigenvalues a_eta,a_eta,b_eta for the quadratic deficit, all positive when eta>0. Gaussian ellipsoid volume 4pi epsilon^(3/2)/(3a_eta sqrt(b_eta)), six maxima and the exact arclength density give C_eta. When eta/epsilon tends to a finite lambda, localization to the circular equilateral manifold, uniform quadratic expansion and orthonormal Jacobian sqrt(3) yield the positive-part phase integral F(s). The integral has the displayed piecewise evaluation, with limiting circle coefficient 4/(3pi). Numerical finite-difference Hessians, direct triangle area evaluations and low-discrepancy rare-event quadrature reproduce both regimes (verify_trilobe.py); only the analytical argument proves the limits.

A general local Laplace principle can explain the fixed-eta exponent but does not itself give the explicit crossover or the sharp phase cutoff without the new calculations.

value.rationale: The lowest nontrivial threefold radial perturbation singles out exactly the three vertices of a maximizing equilateral triangle, so it is a natural symmetry-breaking family rather than an arbitrary parameter slice. Its fixed nonzero deformation replaces the classical linear upper-area tail by an epsilon^(3/2) law; the explicitly computed simultaneous limit identifies exactly when all rotational phases cease to contribute and gives a sharp piecewise arccosine profile. This resolves a natural singular-perturbation gap in near-maximal random inscribed polygons and supplies nontrivial geometric constants useful when comparing nearly circular boundaries. It does not rely on a merely small numerical improvement.
